title: https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-sets-coverage-for-astronaut-anil-menon-launch-to-space-station/
input:
Additionally, the research activities that Menon will undertake during his stay on the station may contribute to advancing human space exploration and potentially benefiting life on Earth. 
Furthermore, it is worth noting that his research efforts will focus on refining in-space production methods for semiconductor crystals, which can often enable the large-scale manufacturing of components needed for various applications. 
Notably, this may include the production of high-performance computers, artificial intelligence systems, and improved medical devices, which tends to rely on such components. 
In essence, Menon's research may also involve the use of ultrasound technology, augmented reality, and artificial intelligence methods, which appears to have the potential to eliminate the need for medical support from Earth on future space missions. 
Ultimately, his participation as a test subject may help researchers understand how blood flow is affected in space, which can often inform the development of protective measures for future astronauts. 
It is worth noting that Menon will also be involved in testing bioprinting vascular constructs in microgravity, which may improve understanding of the aging process and potentially advance therapeutic developments. 
Furthermore, the International Space Station has been continuously occupied by people for more than 25 years, during which time numerous scientific knowledge advancements and research breakthroughs have been made, which may not have been possible on Earth. 
In addition, the space station tends to provide a unique environment for NASA to understand and overcome the challenges of human spaceflight, and may also facilitate the expansion of commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit. 
Ultimately, the research and activities conducted on the space station may build on the foundation for long-duration missions to the Moon and Mars, as part of the Artemis program, and may contribute to advancing human space exploration. 
Ultimately, this highlights the significance of the International Space Station as a platform for scientific research and technological development, and summarises the importance of the research activities being undertaken by Menon and others on the station.
human:
During his stay on the station, Menon will conduct scientific research and technology demonstrations aimed at advancing human space exploration and benefiting life on Earth. He will continue research to refine in-space production of semiconductor crystals to enable the large-scale manufacturing of components needed for high-performance computers, artificial intelligence, and improved medical devices. Menon also will perform ultrasound using augmented reality and artificial intelligence methods that could eliminate the need for medical support from Earth on future space missions. He will be a test subject helping researchers understand how blood flow is affected in space to protect future astronauts. He also will test bioprinting vascular constructs in microgravity to improve understanding of the aging process to advance therapeutic developments.

title: https://www.nasa.gov/solar-system/planets/mars/nasa-discovery-reveals-complex-water-systems-on-early-mars/
input:
In September 2023, when NASA’s Perseverance rover arrived at the inner edge of Mars’ Jezero Crater, mission scientists experienced surprise regarding their discoveries. This geologic area, referred to as the “Margin Unit,” extends along the ancient shoreline of a Martian lake. The scientists anticipated the presence of sedimentary rocks, which typically form as layers of sand accumulate over extended periods. It is worth noting that sedimentary rocks on Earth, which consist of clay and silt, tend to preserve evidence of past microbial life effectively. Furthermore, the scientists expressed particular interest in the strong signals of carbonate minerals that had been detected by Mars orbiters, as these minerals frequently form in environments on Earth that can support life, such as shallow oceans and lakes.

Contrary to their expectations, the rover team identified igneous rock, which can form either from magma located deep underground or from volcanic activity at the surface. Igneous rocks serve as exceptional record-keepers due to the presence of mineral crystals that encapsulate details about their formation. This situation allowed for the preservation of a remarkably intricate record of water activity on early Mars. Notably, the rocks demonstrated evidence of having interacted with water on at least three distinct occasions, with each event contributing to changes in their chemistry and physical appearance. The results of these findings were published on a Monday in the journal Communications Earth & Environment.

Additionally, the instrument responsible for these findings is known as SuperCam, which is situated on the rover’s mast. This instrument determines the mineralogical composition of geologic features based on the light they reflect. When the science team identifies a rock of interest, they can issue commands for SuperCam to project its laser at distances of up to 21 feet (6.5 meters). The spectrum produced by the resulting plasma provides insights into the target’s chemical composition. To date, Perseverance has conducted analyses of more than 185 bedrock targets within this unit using this method. Ultimately, these insights contribute to a deeper understanding of Mars' geological history and potential habitability.

input:
Before the research team arrived at the Margin Unit, the primary hypothesis, which was derived from orbital observations, suggested that the carbonate identified from orbit had formed as a result of interactions with a lake that once existed in Jezero Crater. Candice Bedford, a research scientist affiliated with Purdue University in West Lafayette, Indiana, and the lead author of the study, emphasized that recent findings confirm this location has evolved into a significant crossroads for various aqueous systems. It is important to note that the findings related to the Margin Unit are particularly significant due to Jezero Crater's position within one of the largest exposures of carbonate on Mars; therefore, the insights gained from this research extend well beyond the confines of this specific crater.

Furthermore, Perseverance conducted an exploration of the Margin Unit across an elevation spanning approximately 870 feet, or 265 meters. At elevated regions, the rover discovered rock that displayed coarse-grained and crystalline characteristics, which are indicative of the mineral olivine, and there was minimal evidence suggesting that water had ever been in contact with this rock. Composed of magnesium and iron, the olivine unit in this area originated from a body of magma situated deep underground, where it cooled sufficiently to allow its grains to grow large before eventually reaching the surface due to the erosion of the overlying material. In contrast, lower in the unit, situated on the lakebed, the rock exhibited signs of transformation, as the olivine grains appeared fractured with silica interspersed between them.

Moreover, carbonate and silica minerals serve as essential indicators in the quest to uncover evidence of ancient life. When water interacts with olivine on Earth, this reaction can result in the release of hydrogen, which may serve as a potential food source for certain microbial life forms. Additionally, this interaction leaves behind carbonate and silica, two minerals that effectively encapsulate traces of the historical existence of such microorganisms. In conclusion, the research conducted at the Margin Unit contributes valuable insights into both the geological history of Mars and the potential for past life on the planet.

The Margin Unit findings are important because Jezero Crater sits inside one of the largest exposures of carbonate on Mars, so what we learn here reaches well beyond this crater.”

Perseverance explored the Margin Unit across approximately 870 feet (265 meters) of elevation. At higher elevations, it found rock that was coarse-grained and crystalline — hallmarks of the mineral olivine — with almost no sign that water had ever touched it. Made of magnesium and iron, the area’s olivine unit formed in a body of magma deep underground, cooling slowly enough for its grains to grow large, and reached the surface only after the ground above it eroded away. Lower in the unit, on the lakebed, the rock looks transformed, as the olivine grains were fractured with silica between them.

Carbonate and silica minerals are an important signpost in the search for ancient life. When water interacts with olivine on Earth, the reaction can release hydrogen, which can be a food source for some microbes, and it leaves behind carbonate and silica, two minerals that lock in traces of the past existence of those microbes.

title: https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-sets-coverage-for-astronaut-anil-menon-launch-to-space-station/
input:
NASA astronaut Anil Menon is scheduled to launch on the Roscosmos Soyuz MS-29 spacecraft to the International Space Station on Tuesday, July 14. He will be accompanied by cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina, and their mission aims to support the scientific research efforts of Expedition 74. 

It is worth noting that Menon, Dubrov, and Kikina will lift off at 10:47 a.m. EDT, which corresponds to 7:47 p.m. Baikonur time, from the Baikonur Cosmodrome located in Kazakhstan. Furthermore, live coverage of the launch and subsequent docking will be accessible on various platforms, including NASA+, Amazon Prime, and the agency's YouTube channel. This highlights the availability of NASA content across multiple online channels, including social media.

Following a two-orbit journey lasting approximately three hours, the spacecraft is expected to dock automatically at 1:56 p.m. with the Prichal module. input: Additionally, it is worth noting that the Perseverance team can determine the sequence of the Margin Unit’s interactions with water, but not their age. On the first occasion water reached the rocks of the Margin Unit, carbon-dioxide-rich groundwater reacted with olivine, resulting in ridges of carbonate that run through the fractures in bedrock at low elevations. Today, these carbonate-filled fractures are left standing as the softer rock around them wears away. Furthermore, according to Eleni Ravanis, a planetary scientist at the University of Hawaii at Manoa and a coauthor of the study, some of the Margin Unit rocks also contain silica. The transformation of olivine into carbonate can leave silica behind, and more of that silica appears to be present in rocks that sat below the water line. Subsequently, a water event occurred that generated mineral veins at one location in the eastern part of the Margin Unit, about 10 inches (25 centimeters) thick, creating minerals like calcium sulfate and fluorite. It is worth noting that the discovery of fluorite constitutes an important clue, because it typically forms when hot water circulates through volcanic rocks, revealing that this area experienced a later, heated underground-water event. Moreover, according to Bedford, if there is one thing he has learned after 10 years working with Mars rovers, it is that Mars constantly throws surprises at researchers. It is very rare that things are as expected from orbital data, and it is hoped that this work helps reshape how scientists view the history of water in Jezero Crater and across Mars. Ultimately, it is hoped that this work helps planetary scientists reconstruct the changing climate and habitability of early Mars. Additionally, a key objective of Perseverance’s mission on Mars is astrobiology, including the search for signs of ancient microbial life. Furthermore, the rover characterizes the planet’s geology and past climate and collects and stores Martian rock and regolith. In essence, the findings shed light on the sequence of watery events in the Margin Unit, even if their precise timing remains uncertain.

input:
NASA is set to provide live coverage of the launch and subsequent docking of a Roscosmos cargo spacecraft, which is expected to transport approximately three tons of essential food, fuel, and supplies intended for the crew residing aboard the International Space Station. 

It is important to note that the uncrewed Progress 96 resupply spacecraft is scheduled to initiate its launch at 9:33 a.m. EDT, corresponding to 6:33 p.m. Baikonur time, on Wednesday, September 16. This launch will occur on a Soyuz rocket from the Baikonur Cosmodrome located in Kazakhstan, and NASA's live coverage of the launch will commence at 9:15 a.m. 

Following a journey lasting three days to reach the space station, the Progress spacecraft is projected to autonomously dock with the space-facing port of the Poisk module at 9:46 a.m. on Saturday, September 19. Furthermore, NASA will begin its coverage of the arrival at 9 a.m. on that date. 

The spacecraft is anticipated to remain attached to the orbiting laboratory for a duration of approximately five months before it departs to re-enter Earth's atmosphere, where it is expected to incinerate harmlessly over the Pacific Ocean. 

It is worth noting that prior to the arrival of Progress 96, the Progress 94 spacecraft undocked from the space station at 11:18 a.m. on September 7, which was followed by its departure and subsequent destructive re-entry. 

In summary, for more than 25 years, individuals have continuously inhabited and worked aboard the International Space Station, contributing to the advancement of scientific knowledge and achieving research breakthroughs that may not be possible on Earth. The space station serves as a crucial platform for NASA as it seeks to understand and address the challenges associated with human spaceflight, expand commercial opportunities in low Earth orbit, and lay the groundwork for long-duration missions to the Moon, as part of the Artemis program, and ultimately to Mars.

title: https://www.nasa.gov/communicating-with-missions/
input:
Science and exploration are significantly enhanced through various initiatives. The Space Communications and Navigation (SCaN) Program is responsible for the operation and management of communication and navigation systems that are essential for every mission conducted by NASA. It is worth noting that NASA's extensive antennas on Earth transmit and receive spacecraft commands, unique images, and scientific data on a daily basis. This capability facilitates critical connections between missions, such as the Voyager mission, which investigates regions beyond our solar system, and astronauts aboard the International Space Station, thereby establishing vital communication links with our home planet.

Furthermore, astronauts onboard the International Space Station, missions that monitor Earth, as well as spacecraft engaged in the exploration of the Moon and beyond, rely on NASA’s Near Space Network for navigation and communication services. The network employs a combination of government and commercial resources, supporting scientific and exploratory missions by returning terabytes of essential data each day.

Moreover, the Deep Space Network (DSN) represents NASA’s global network of large radio communication antennas, featuring dish diameters of 34 and 70 meters. These antennas are strategically located in Goldstone, California, Madrid, Spain, and Canberra, Australia. The DSN plays a crucial role in supporting communication and navigation for spacecraft operating at the Moon, Mars, and beyond, while its planetary radar and radio astronomy capabilities assist scientists in gaining a deeper understanding of our solar system and the universe.

In addition, SCaN actively contributes to NASA’s efforts in the exploration of the Moon, Mars, and other celestial bodies. The program’s lunar initiatives include providing communication and navigation support for the Artemis missions, which aim to deliver internet-like functionalities to the lunar surface while enhancing search and rescue capabilities for astronauts.

It is worth noting that SCaN is in the process of transforming its near-space communication services and actively engaging with the commercial sector to facilitate both direct-to-Earth and space relay communication services. By fostering public-private partnerships, SCaN is embracing new opportunities that contribute to the development of a secure and interoperable communications ecosystem.

Ultimately, SCaN’s global network is sustained through ongoing modernization efforts and strategic partnerships, which ensure dependable support for current and future missions while integrating commercial services that expand capacity and reduce costs. This cohesive approach serves to enhance the capabilities of NASA's communication and navigation systems, thereby advancing the frontiers of exploration.

title: https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/president-honors-nasas-artemis-ii-crew-with-highest-us-space-award/
input:
The Congressional Space Medal of Honor was established by Congress in 1969 to acknowledge astronauts who have distinguished themselves through exceptional bravery and meritorious contributions to the well-being of both the nation and humanity. Since the inception of the space program, a total of 34 individuals have been awarded this honor, including the crews of Apollo 1, Challenger, and Columbia, who received the recognition posthumously. 

It is worth noting that NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman stated that under President Trump’s guidance, America has been positioned to regain its leadership in the global space sector. This has been demonstrated through initiatives such as the Artemis program, which has provided NASA with the necessary resources and direction to compete in the current space race. Furthermore, he highlighted the extraordinary skill and bravery exhibited by the Artemis II crew, showcasing what American leadership and exploration can achieve at their best. This accomplishment was facilitated by the exemplary efforts of the NASA workforce, in conjunction with industry collaborators and international partners, illustrating the potential for significant achievements when there is a commitment to ambitious objectives. 

Ultimately, the first crewed mission of NASA’s Artemis program has set the stage for the planned Artemis III test flight in 2027, which aims to validate rendezvous and docking capabilities between the Orion spacecraft and commercial human landing systems. This will be followed by the Artemis IV mission in 2028, which is intended to return American astronauts to the lunar surface, marking a significant milestone in ongoing space exploration efforts. Overall, these initiatives emphasize a renewed focus on exploring and establishing a sustained human presence on the Moon.

There now are 34 recipients of the award since the beginning of the space program, including the crews of Apollo 1, Challenger, and Columbia who received the award posthumously.

“President Trump’s leadership has put America back on a path to lead the world in space, from creating the Artemis program to giving NASA the resources and mandate to win this new space race,” said NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman. “The Artemis II crew answered that call with extraordinary skill and courage, showing the world the Moon again and what American leadership and exploration look like at their best. Their achievement was made possible by the exceptional NASA workforce, alongside our industry and international partners, who showed once again what can be accomplished when we commit to big, bold endeavors. We will build on this success as we return to the lunar surface and establish an enduring presence on the Moon.”

The first crewed mission under NASA’s Artemis program paved the way for the 2027 Artemis III test flight in low Earth orbit to demonstrate rendezvous and docking capabilities between Orion and commercial human landing systems, and the Artemis IV mission in 2028, which will return American astronauts to the lunar surface.

Since the space program started, 34 people have received this award, including the crews of Apollo 1, Challenger, and Columbia, who got it after they died.  

NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said that under President Trump, the U.S. is ready to take the lead in space again. This is shown by projects like Artemis, which has given NASA the money and plan to compete in the space race. He also praised the skill and bravery of the Artemis II crew, showing what America can do when it leads in space. This was because of the hard work of NASA staff and others who helped, showing that big goals can be achieved with teamwork.  

The first crewed Artemis mission has set up the way for Artemis III in 2027, which will test how the Orion space capsule works with commercial landing systems. Then Artemis IV in 2028 will send astronauts back to the Moon, a big step in space exploration. These plans show the U.S. is focusing on staying on the Moon long-term.

title: https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-astronaut-anil-menon-crewmates-arrive-at-space-station/
input: NASA astronaut Anil Menon, together with Roscosmos cosmonauts Pyotr Dubrov and Anna Kikina, arrived safely at the International Space Station on Tuesday. This arrival brings the crew of the orbiting laboratory to a total of 10 individuals for approximately the next two weeks. The trio launched aboard the Soyuz MS-29 spacecraft at 10:47 a.m. EDT, which corresponds to 7:47 p.m. local time, from the Baikonur Cosmodrome in Kazakhstan. After a journey lasting three hours and encompassing two orbits, the spacecraft docked at 1:52 p.m. with the station's Prichal module. Following the opening of the hatch, which is expected at about 4 p.m., the new arrivals will be welcomed by the space station Expedition 74 crew. This crew includes NASA astronauts Jessica Meir, Jack Hathaway, and Chris Williams, along with ESA astronaut Sophie Adenot and Roscosmos cosmonauts Sergey Kud-Sverchkov, Sergei Mikaev, and Andrey Fedyaev. NASA's live coverage of the hatch opening is scheduled to begin at 3:30 p.m. on NASA+, Amazon Prime, and YouTube. It is worth noting that individuals can learn how to watch NASA content through a variety of online platforms, including social media. During his stay aboard the station, Menon will conduct scientific research and technology demonstrations aimed at advancing human space exploration and benefiting life on Earth. He will continue research to refine in-space production of semiconductor crystals, which may enable the large-scale manufacturing of components needed for high-performance computers, artificial intelligence, and improved medical devices. Additionally, Menon will perform ultrasound using augmented reality and artificial intelligence methods that could eliminate the need for medical support from Earth on future space missions. He will serve as a test subject helping researchers understand how blood flow is affected in space to protect future astronauts. Furthermore, he will test bioprinting vascular constructs in microgravity to improve understanding of the aging process to advance therapeutic developments. Expedition 75 is scheduled to begin on Sunday, July 26, following the departure of Williams, Kud-Sverchkov, and Mikaev, as they conclude an eight-month science mission aboard the orbital outpost. Ultimately, this highlights the continuous rotation of crews and the ongoing scientific work on the station.

title: https://www.nasa.gov/blogs/spacestation/2026/09/22/station-nears-upcoming-crew-swap-during-biomedicine-cargo-duties/
input:
Notably, four members of the Expedition 75 crew are preparing for their return to Earth aboard a SpaceX Dragon vehicle next month, while their replacement crew is simultaneously preparing for launch. Furthermore, the residents aboard the International Space Station are continuing their research in biomedicine, activating Earth imagery equipment, and unpacking supplies from a cargo spacecraft.

It is worth noting that NASA's SpaceX Crew-12 mission launched on February 13, carrying NASA astronauts Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, European Space Agency astronaut Sophie Adenot, and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev to the orbital outpost the following day. The four crew members are now approaching the conclusion of their mission as they await the arrival of the Crew-13 mission, which is expected to occur in early October.

Additionally, Meir and Hathaway, who serve as the Crew-12 commander and pilot respectively, alternated on Tuesday between training on a computer and reviewing the procedures necessary for their imminent undocking from the station and subsequent descent into Earth's atmosphere inside the Dragon vehicle. Subsequently, the duo collaborated with Crew-12 mission specialists Adenot and Fedyaev to check the pressure suits they will utilize during their return to Earth, culminating in a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean. The four crew members confirmed the appropriate fit of the suits, tested the functionality of the communication systems, and conducted inspections to assess the overall condition of the suits.

In addition, Meir gathered emergency breathing equipment in preparation for the arrival of Crew-13. She meticulously inspected the masks, installed filter cartridges, and organized them in bags to ensure quick access. The standard operating procedure dictates that the masks will be stowed inside the Dragon vehicle following the arrival of Crew-13. Moreover, Meir participated with her returning crewmates in taking waist and leg measurements, subsequently entering the data into the EveryWear application on a computer tablet prior to trying on their Dragon pressure suits. In summary, the preparations are extensive as the crew members ready themselves for their upcoming transition back to Earth.

input:
Furthermore, the standards encompass the computer code for encryption algorithms, the guidelines for their implementation, and their intended applications, representing the culmination of an eight-year initiative overseen by NIST, which has a notable history of encryption development. The agency has mobilized global experts in cryptography to conceptualize, submit, and subsequently assess various cryptographic algorithms that may withstand the challenges posed by quantum computing. While this emerging technology has the potential to bring transformative changes to a variety of fields, including weather forecasting, fundamental physics, and drug design, it also introduces certain risks.

It is worth noting that Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology and NIST Director Laurie E. Locascio stated that quantum computing technology has the potential to address some of society's most difficult challenges, and the newly established standards reflect NIST's dedication to preventing any simultaneous threats to our security. The finalized standards can be viewed as the pinnacle of NIST's commitment to protecting our sensitive electronic information.

In essence, encryption plays a crucial role in contemporary digital society by safeguarding vast amounts of electronic information, including email contents, medical records, and photo collections, along with information that is essential for national security. Encrypted data is capable of being transmitted across public computer networks, remaining inaccessible to everyone except the sender and the intended recipient.

Additionally, encryption mechanisms rely on intricate mathematical problems that traditional computers often encounter as exceedingly challenging or beyond their capabilities. However, a sufficiently advanced quantum computer could potentially analyze numerous possible solutions to these problems in a remarkably efficient manner, thereby undermining existing encryption methods. The algorithms standardized by NIST are derived from alternative mathematical challenges that may prove difficult for both traditional and quantum computers to resolve. Overall, this comprehensive approach aims to enhance the security of electronic information in an increasingly complex digital landscape.

The nascent technology could revolutionize fields from weather forecasting to fundamental physics to drug design, but it carries threats as well.

“Quantum computing technology could become a force for solving many of society’s most intractable problems, and the new standards represent NIST’s commitment to ensuring it will not simultaneously disrupt our security,” said Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology and NIST Director Laurie E. Locascio. “These finalized standards are the capstone of NIST’s efforts to safeguard our confidential electronic information.”

Encryption tools rely on complex math problems that conventional computers find difficult or impossible to solve. A sufficiently capable quantum computer, though, would be able to sift through a vast number of potential solutions to these problems very quickly, thereby defeating current encryption. While quantum computing has the potential to transform weather forecasting, basic physics, and drug design, it also poses risks.

“Quantum computing technology has the potential to solve some of society’s hardest problems, and the new standards reflect NIST’s commitment to preventing any quantum computing threats to our security,” said Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology and NIST Director Laurie E. Locascio. “These finalized standards represent the pinnacle of NIST’s effort to protect our sensitive electronic information.”

Encryption protects billions of electronic pieces of information today, from the contents of your email and medical records to your photo collection and information that is critical to our national security. Encrypted data can be sent across the public computer network, but only the sender and the recipient can read it.

Encryption mechanisms rely on complex mathematical problems that traditional computers find extremely difficult or impossible to solve. But a powerful enough quantum computer could look at all possible solutions to these problems quickly and efficiently, breaking existing encryption methods. The algorithms standardized by NIST are based on other mathematical problems that would be difficult for both traditional and quantum computers to solve.

title: https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2024/01/nist-and-nsf-award-nearly-71-million-15-universities-support-disaster
input:
The University of California, Los Angeles has proposed a project with a budget of $399,933 aimed at utilizing principles from artificial intelligence to create near real-time models for predicting infrastructure damage in the immediate aftermath of significant hazard events, such as wildfires, earthquakes, and floods. This initiative may enhance the phases of emergency response and recovery planning that follow these events.

Furthermore, the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign has set a budget of $399,851 to investigate how various characteristics of thunderstorm winds, particularly peak wind speeds designated for design levels, are related to the different mechanisms that generate such winds. This project may also examine the spatial variabilities and temporal intermittencies associated with these generating mechanisms.

Additionally, the University of Mississippi has requested $399,475 to establish a standardized monitoring approach for impoundments of mine tailings, which are substantial geotechnical structures that store mining waste. This approach could potentially revolutionize the monitoring of infrastructure and the management of hazards during extreme weather conditions.

Notably, North Carolina State University has a proposal with a budget of $398,891 that seeks to advance the understanding of how local erosion events may contribute to flooding in adjacent communities. This project also aims to explore how these floods can be managed by permitting sections of barriers to revert to their natural state and how this transformation, when informed and deliberated upon by community stakeholders, may influence the meanings associated with community places.

Moreover, Johns Hopkins University has proposed a project with a budget of $391,951 focused on developing a novel system for providing rapid, scalable, and joint assessments of cascading hazards, such as ground shaking, landslides, and liquefaction during seismic events, by leveraging the causal dependencies that exist among these hazards.

In addition, George Mason University seeks $385,353 to evaluate the impact of extreme heat on the effectiveness of disinfection processes in drinking water distribution systems and to assess an innovative engineering solution that may enhance resiliency to extreme heat disasters.

Lastly, Oklahoma State University has proposed a project with a budget of $367,706 aimed at investigating the potential influence of social networks and micromobility options, such as bicycles and scooters, on improving the planning and operation of resilience hubs. This infrastructural concept has the capacity to support more equitable disaster response and recovery efforts. 

In summary, these initiatives from various universities aim to enhance understanding and develop solutions for infrastructure resilience and disaster management in the face of extreme weather events and hazards.

Laurie E. Locascio, under secretary of commerce for standards and technology and director of the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), has been elected to the National Academy of Engineering — one of the highest professional distinctions accorded to an engineer.

Locascio leads NIST’s collaborative efforts with industry, academia and government to unleash U.S. innovation by advancing technology, measurements and standards. A key priority for her is the successful implementation of the CHIPS for America initiative, a $50 billion suite of programs to strengthen and revitalize U.S. leadership in semiconductor research, development and manufacturing.

In addition, Locascio is working to advance and grow NIST’s work in critical emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence, quantum information science, cybersecurity and privacy, biotechnology, energy and advanced communications. She also promotes NIST’s continuing role in advancing federal and international standards, which helps ensure U.S. economic competitiveness and technology leadership.

Before being confirmed as NIST director in April 2022, Locascio served as vice president for research at the University of Maryland College Park and University of Maryland Baltimore. Prior to that, she worked at NIST for 31 years, starting as a research biomedical engineer and rising to lead the agency’s Material Measurement Laboratory. She also served as the acting associate director for laboratory programs, the No. 2 position at NIST, providing direction and operational guidance for NIST’s research programs.

Locascio has published 115 scientific papers and has received 12 patents in the fields of bioengineering and analytical chemistry. She is a fellow of the American Association for the Advancement of Science, the American Chemical Society, the American Institute for Medical and Biological Engineering, and the National Academy of Inventors.

Notably, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) intends to pursue this objective in collaboration with the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), which is also working with the Gates Foundation.

Furthermore, it is important to recognize that multiple volatile organic compounds (VOCs) are often implicated in these diseases, which suggests that disease-diagnosing breathalyzers may need to be significantly more advanced than the breathalyzer devices used by law enforcement for detecting drivers under the influence of alcohol. That particular test is designed to detect only a single compound in the breath, specifically ethanol.

For nearly a decade, NIST researchers have also been investigating the feasibility of creating a breathalyzer test for recent cannabis use. title: https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2022/07/nist-develops-genetic-material-validating-mpox-tests
input: Additionally, it is worth noting that Victoria Olson, who serves as the CDC’s deputy director of laboratory science and safety, has stated that positive control materials can often be critical for ensuring the reliability of diagnostic tests. Furthermore, she indicated that having a reliable supply of high-quality control material from a trusted source such as NIST may help the agency mount an effective testing program more quickly. In essence, the NIST control material is a liquid solution that contains partial sequences from nine mpox genes, which are strung together into molecules of DNA that are roughly 3,400 base pairs, or letter pairs, long. Notably, the value of the NIST control material does not tend to reside in the DNA itself, which is relatively easy to synthesize. Rather, it appears to reside in NIST’s assurance that each vial of the material contains the same very precisely measured amount of DNA, to a known degree of certainty. To illustrate, each microliter tends to contain 110,000 copies of the DNA strand, plus or minus 10 percent. Additionally, NIST scientists analyzed the DNA in order to ensure that there are no errors in the genetic sequences. Furthermore, they measured the concentration of DNA in the material through the use of a high-precision technique that is called digital PCR. Moreover, they worked with NIST statisticians in order to ensure that each microliter of the material contains the same amount of DNA, within the stated bounds of uncertainty. Scott Jackson, who is the NIST microbial geneticist that led the effort, has said that they do a lot of work in order to make sure that they get those numbers right. On June 22, the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services announced that it would authorize commercial laboratories to conduct mpox tests, which previously were only conducted by a limited number of public laboratories. In addition, commercial laboratories can use the material from NIST in order to validate their tests and to determine test sensitivity, which is the lowest amount of genetic material that their tests can detect. Ultimately, the availability of this well-characterized NIST control material may serve to support more reliable and more rapidly implemented mpox testing across a range of laboratory settings.

title: https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2025/01/nist-database-can-help-increase-recycling-textiles-and-clothing
input:
At those centers, workers engage in the sorting of clothing by utilizing handheld devices that emit near-infrared light. These devices are capable of measuring the extent to which the light either passes through or scatters off the fabric, thereby generating a distinctive pattern that functions as a sort of fingerprint. This unique identifier can be instrumental in recognizing the types of fibers present in the clothing. This process, known as near-infrared (NIR) spectroscopy, also finds application in automated conveyor belt systems; however, it is important to note that current techniques still necessitate substantial manual labor.

In recent years, manufacturers of recycling equipment have increasingly integrated machine learning and artificial intelligence into the enhancement of their sorting algorithms. In order to effectively train these algorithms, high-quality reference data is essential.

This is where the National Institute of Standards and Technology’s (NIST) database becomes significant. This database, referred to as the Near-Infrared Spectra of Origin-defined and Real-world Textiles, or NIR-SORT, encompasses 64 distinct types of fabric along with the corresponding NIR fingerprints they yield. The database includes pure fiber types such as cotton and polyester, blended fiber types such as spandex blends, and real-world fabrics sourced from thrift stores. Manufacturers of NIR scanner systems can utilize this database to train and evaluate their sorting algorithms, thereby enhancing the performance of their products.

Notably, challenges arise when fibers exhibit similarities, such as cotton and hemp, leading to comparable near-infrared signals. The same issue applies to cotton and polyester blends, raising the question of whether a given sample is a new fiber or a blend of two or more fibers. Katarina Goodge, a NIST research chemist who spearheaded the development of the database, emphasizes that artificial intelligence has the potential to refine the decision-making process, thereby increasing accuracy.

Given that NIST serves as the nation’s measurement institute, it possesses both the equipment and the expertise necessary to populate this database with exceptionally high-quality spectral data. This advancement may lead to a reduction in errors associated with fabric identification, ultimately facilitating a greater volume of textiles being recycled. In summary, the integration of this sophisticated database and advanced technology appears to signify a promising step forward for the textile recycling industry.

title: https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2024/09/nist-awards-3-million-community-based-cybersecurity-workforce-development
input:
In Gaithersburg, Maryland, it is noteworthy that the U.S. Department of Commerce’s National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) has allocated nearly $3 million through cooperative agreements aimed at developing a workforce that may be necessary for the protection of the nation’s organizations and infrastructure against cybersecurity threats. Furthermore, grants of approximately $200,000 each are expected to reach 15 educational and community organizations across 11 states, which are working to address what appears to be a significant shortage of qualified cybersecurity professionals.

Additionally, the oversight of these cooperative agreements will be managed by NICE, a collaborative initiative led by NIST that involves partnerships between government, educational institutions, and the private sector, with a focus on enhancing cybersecurity education, training, and the development of a diverse workforce.

It is worth noting that Laurie E. Locascio, the Under Secretary of Commerce for Standards and Technology and NIST Director, emphasized the importance of a highly skilled cybersecurity workforce for strengthening national and economic security. She stated that this investment in cybersecurity education and training may help to fulfill a critical workforce gap while providing individuals with the necessary skills to thrive in well-paying, quality jobs.

In addition, the NICE-funded CyberSeek tool, which analyzes trends within the cybersecurity job market, discovered that there were nearly 470,000 job openings in the U.S. from May 2023 to April 2024. During this period, it was reported that approximately 85 workers were available to fill every 100 cybersecurity positions in the country, suggesting a potential ongoing challenge in matching job supply with demand.

Moreover, the organizations that receive these awards will establish Regional Alliances and Multistakeholder Partnerships to Stimulate (RAMPS) projects aimed at promoting cybersecurity education and workforce development. These RAMPS initiatives are intended to coordinate the workforce requirements of local businesses and nonprofit organizations with the NICE Workforce Framework for Cybersecurity.

Ultimately, Rodney Petersen, the NICE Director, indicated that the RAMPS program is designed to provide individuals from a variety of backgrounds, experiences, and life circumstances with access to careers in cybersecurity. He further highlighted that this initiative encourages collaboration within communities to create pathways to quality jobs for all Americans while also contributing to local and regional economic development by addressing workforce needs.

title: https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2024/01/nist-and-nsf-award-nearly-71-million-15-universities-support-disaster
input:
In Gaithersburg, Maryland, the United States Department of Commerce’s National Institute of Standards and Technology, alongside the National Science Foundation, has awarded nearly $7.1 million in financial grants aimed at enhancing the capacity of buildings, infrastructure, and communities to effectively withstand severe natural hazards. These projects receive funding through the Disaster Resilience Research Grant program, which is jointly administered by NIST and NSF. 

It is worth noting that these grants promote scientifically grounded methods to enhance resilience, which encompass improved planning, policy formulation, decision-making processes, design considerations, and the establishment of codes and standards. Joannie Chin, the director of NIST’s Engineering Laboratory, emphasized that these initiatives can also facilitate the education of the next generation of engineers and designers, while ensuring that diverse communities are taken into account and provided with the necessary tools to safeguard their futures.

Furthermore, applicants were encouraged to explore various natural hazards, including hurricanes, tornadoes, sustained rainfall, coastal flooding, inland flooding, tsunamis, wildland-urban interface fires, and earthquakes, with the objective of identifying strategies that communities may employ to mitigate their vulnerabilities and enhance their resilience to these phenomena.

Moreover, Susan Margulies, the assistant director for engineering at NSF, articulated that the investment from NSF is intended to diminish the significant economic and societal repercussions associated with natural hazards. The collaboration with NIST aims to expedite the implementation of innovative ideas and methodologies into planning processes, building codes, and decision-making frameworks, ultimately fortifying the nation’s resilience against natural hazards.

The University of Notre Dame will receive $400,000 to enhance the accuracy of predictions regarding the potential impacts of storm wave or current-carried debris on elevated structures, thereby supporting the objectives of the American Society of Civil Engineers’ Flood Loads Subcommittee. In addition, the University of Delaware is set to receive $399,988 to deepen the understanding of risks related to acute care access and flooding impacts, with the goal of enhancing disaster preparedness among service providers and communities, ultimately ensuring continuity of care and reducing morbidity and mortality linked to treatment disruptions during future disasters. Overall, these initiatives represent a significant investment in the resilience of communities facing natural hazards.

input:
It is worth noting that the most advanced reference genome prior to the T2T version may lack approximately 8 percent of the genome, and certain sections, which can often pose challenges for sequencing technologies, tend to be filled with errors. These imperfections made the reference genome resemble a puzzle box picture that contains missing segments and displays pieces that are arranged incorrectly. However, due to significant technological and scientific advancements in the field of genomics over the past two decades, the T2T consortium was able to enhance and refine the human reference genome.

Furthermore, the team identified an effective platform for the reference in the 1000 Genomes Project (1KGP), which is an international initiative that has compiled genetically diverse genome sequences from thousands of individuals across four continents. Rather than initiating a new collection of DNA samples from additional subjects, the researchers could effectively assemble the DNA segments that had already been documented by the 1KGP effort.

Additionally, the authors employed computer programs to analyze a total of 3,202 genomes in conjunction with the T2T reference. They subsequently compared these results to previously published work conducted on these genomes using the earlier reference. It became evident that genomes compiled with either of the two references exhibited significant differences in critical regions.

Notably, the T2T reference genome illuminated millions of genetic variations—segments of DNA that vary among individuals—that the previous reference had overlooked. It also corrected tens of thousands of inaccuracies in the sequences, such as improperly located variations. In essence, the new genetic variations filled in the missing segments of the puzzle box picture, while the corrections ensured that the puzzle pieces were accurately positioned where thousands had previously been misaligned. Overall, the advancements represented by the T2T reference genome contribute significantly to our understanding of human genetics.

title: https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2023/05/nist-team-demonstrates-novel-way-convert-heat-electricity
input:
Researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) have developed a new device that may significantly enhance the process of converting heat into electricity. If this technology is further refined, it can potentially help recover some of the heat energy that is lost in the United States, which amounts to approximately $100 billion annually.

Notably, the innovative fabrication technique, which has been introduced by NIST researcher Kris Bertness along with her colleagues, involves the deposition of numerous microscopic columns made from gallium nitride on a silicon wafer. Subsequently, layers of silicon are removed from the bottom side of the wafer, leaving behind only a thin sheet of the material. The interaction between the columns and the silicon sheet tends to slow down the heat transfer within the silicon, thereby enabling a greater portion of the heat to be converted into electrical current. Bertness and her team from the University of Colorado Boulder shared their findings in the journal Advanced Materials on March 23.

Once this fabrication method reaches its full potential, it is conceivable that the silicon sheets could be applied around steam or exhaust pipes, allowing for the conversion of heat emissions into electricity that may be used to power nearby devices or integrated into a power grid. Furthermore, another possible application could involve the cooling of computer chips.

In essence, the study conducted by NIST and the University of Colorado is grounded in an intriguing phenomenon first identified by the German physicist Thomas Seebeck. During the early 1820s, Seebeck was investigating two metal wires, each composed of different materials, which were connected at both ends to form a loop. It is worth noting that when the two junctions of the wires were maintained at differing temperatures, a nearby compass needle exhibited a deflection. Subsequent researchers realized that this deflection occurred as a result of the temperature difference inducing a voltage between the two sections, leading to a flow of current from the hotter area to the cooler one. This current subsequently generated a magnetic field, which caused the compass needle to deflect. Ultimately, this historical discovery lays the foundation for the modern advancements being explored in heat-to-electricity conversion technology.

title: https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2022/07/out-shadows-new-imaging-method-reveals-concealed-objects
input:
Other methods that do not rely on a light source analyze the shadows created by hidden objects on surfaces or detect the heat, specifically infrared radiation, that is naturally emitted by concealed bodies and scattered into view. However, it is important to note that these techniques often demand substantial computing time and analysis. A good algorithm combined with significant computational power may extract images, yet the quality of these images may not be satisfactory, as mentioned by NIST physicist Erich Grossman.

Furthermore, Grossman and his team have developed a novel approach that focuses on detecting minimal quantities of longer wavelength radiation in the submillimeter range, which exists just beyond microwave radiation. This range, which encompasses wavelengths from 300 micrometers to 1 millimeter, tends to allow walls made from various materials to appear relatively smooth and function as partial mirrors, thereby reflecting rather than diffusely scattering the radiation emitted by hidden objects.

To create an image, it is necessary to direct and focus this reflected radiation. Unlike visible light, which can be manipulated using glass lenses, submillimeter radiation requires different methods for steering. Grossman and his colleagues utilized curved mirrors to concentrate the invisible light effectively.

In their experimental work with the prototype, Grossman and his collaborators at the University of Minnesota Twin Cities in Minneapolis demonstrated the capability to construct images of objects concealed behind walls within approximately 20 minutes. This innovative technique utilizes advanced indium phosphide transistors that amplify submillimeter radiation with minimal noise over a broad range of wavelengths, eliminating the need for complex algorithms or significant computer analysis. Grossman emphasized, "What is noteworthy about this method is its simplicity," as it does not involve quantum mechanics, relativity, or anything sophisticated, relying solely on transistors, a basic computer, and mirrors. Overall, the entire apparatus is compact enough to be carried in a backpack.

title: https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2026/05/shooting-moon-ultrastable-lasers-dark-craters-could-enable-lunar-navigation
input: Additionally, it is worth noting that these craters may possess an even higher vacuum than the lunar surface, which can often further reduce or eliminate vibrations arising from sound waves and stray particles that might strike the mirrors and alter the distance between them. Furthermore, by radiating any residual heat from the cavity system into the much colder abyss of outer space, the optical cavity could be cooled further, without the need for a cryostat or other equipment, to a temperature of 16 K. Moreover, at that temperature, silicon neither expands nor contracts when exposed to tiny changes in temperature, thereby ensuring that light entering the cavity always traverses exactly the same distance between the two mirrors. Once the optical silicon cavity is deployed, a commercially available laser would be placed nearby, either on the rim or inside the permanently shadowed crater. In essence, a small amount of laser light directed into the optical cavity would be used to lock the laser frequency to one of the resonant frequencies allowed by the cavity, ensuring that the laser emits light of a single unchanging color. After stabilizing the frequency of its light, the laser could act as a GPS-like signal, guiding lunar spacecraft to land safely, especially those set to touch down on dimly lit regions near the south pole. Additionally, by tuning its light to the signals of atomic clocks on satellites, a high-stability lunar laser could also form the backbone of the first optical atomic clock on an extraterrestrial surface. Ultimately, this timekeeping signal would rival those from the most precise and accurate optical atomic clocks on Earth, which Ye and colleagues have built in Earth-bound laboratories. In summary, the deployment of such a cavity system appears to offer a promising pathway toward unprecedented timekeeping and navigation capabilities on the lunar surface.

title: https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2022/03/revamped-design-could-take-powerful-biological-computers-test-tube-cell
input:
Additionally, it is worth noting that the synthesis of DNA sequences, which are part of computers known as strand displacement circuits, tends to occur separately and in a double-stranded form, in order to prevent undesired binding. Furthermore, this double-stranded form can often act as a locked gate, which may only unlock if the target sequence comes along and takes the place of one of the strands, thereby reaching a state of binding. Notably, the double strand is characterized by the fact that every chemical base on each strand is bound to a base on the other, which appears to be a crucial aspect of its function.

In essence, the researchers, including Schaffter and Elizabeth Strychalski, leader of NIST's Cellular Engineering Group and co-author of the study, reached a decision to mimic this locked gate function in their RNA circuit, keeping in mind that cells would ultimately have to produce these locked gates themselves. It is worth noting that the researchers wrote the sequences in such a way that one half of the strands could bind with the other half, which tends to result in the RNA sequences folding on themselves, thereby ensuring they are in a locked state. Ultimately, the binding process can often lead to the formation of a locked gate, which may be an important aspect of the circuit's function.

Furthermore, the gates would need to be composed of two chemically bound but distinct strands, which appears to be a necessary condition for their proper functioning. Additionally, the team obtained the double-stranded design in their gates by incorporating a stretch of RNA called a ribozyme near the folding point of the gates, which tends to sever itself after the RNA strand it was embedded in folded, resulting in the creation of two separate strands. In summary, the researchers developed a method to create locked gates in RNA circuits, which may have important implications for the field, and ultimately, the development of these gates tends to depend on the careful design of the RNA sequences and the incorporation of specific elements, such as ribozymes.
human:
To prevent undesired binding, DNA sequences that are part of computers known as strand displacement circuits are usually synthesized (in machines rather than cells) separately and in a double-stranded form. With every chemical base on each strand bound to a base on the other, this double strand acts as a locked gate that would only unlock if the target sequence came along and took the place of one of the strands.

Schaffter and Elizabeth Strychalski, leader of NIST’s Cellular Engineering Group and co-author of the study, sought to mimic this “locked gate” function in their RNA circuit, keeping in mind that, ultimately, cells would have to produce these locked gates themselves. To set cells up for success, the researchers wrote the sequences so that one half of the strands could bind flush with the other half. Binding this way, RNA sequences would fold on themselves like a hotdog bun, ensuring they are in a locked state.

But to work properly, the gates would need to be two chemically bound but distinct strands, more like a hamburger bun or sandwich than a hotdog bun. The team obtained the double-stranded design in their gates by coding in a stretch of RNA called a ribozyme near the folding point of the gates. This particular ribozyme — taken from the genome of a hepatitis virus — would sever itself after the RNA strand it was embedded in folded, creating two separate strands.

DNA sequences used in strand displacement circuits are often synthesized as double strands to avoid unwanted binding. This double-stranded form can act as a locked gate that only opens when the right sequence replaces one strand, allowing binding. Each base in one strand pairs with a base in the other, a key feature of this structure.

Researchers like Schaffter and Elizabeth Strychalski, leader of NIST's Cellular Engineering Group, decided to mimic this locked gate in their RNA circuit. They designed the sequences so the strands could bind, causing the RNA to fold and stay locked. Binding can then form a locked gate, important for the circuit.

The gates need two chemically bound but different strands to work properly. The team used a ribozyme in the RNA to create two separate strands after folding. This method helps build locked gates in RNA circuits, which could be important for future developments. The design of RNA sequences and elements like ribozymes are key to making these gates work.

Consequently, this phenomenon appears to diminish thermal conductivity, thereby increasing the temperature gradient from one end of the material to the other. Furthermore, it is noteworthy that the interaction among the phonons achieves this effect while leaving the electrical conductivity of the silicon sheet largely unaffected.

Additionally, the research team is currently engaged in the development of structures that are composed entirely of silicon, which may feature an improved geometry aimed at enhancing thermoelectric heat recovery. In summary, the research explores the manipulation of phonon interactions within silicon to improve thermal management, with promising implications for energy recovery technologies.

title: https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2024/10/nist-awards-15-million-support-development-regenerative-medicine-standards
input:
The National Institute of Standards and Technology, which operates within the United States Department of Commerce, has reached a decision to award cooperative agreements of up to 1.5 million dollars to two organizations. These agreements are intended to support the creation of curricula and programs that will provide training in standards implementation for both the current and future regenerative medicine workforce. It is worth noting that the recipients of these awards were identified through an open and competitive process that was announced earlier in the year.

Regenerative medicine, which can often be understood to encompass cell therapy, gene therapy, and therapeutic tissue engineering, appears to aim at harnessing the body's innate capacity for healing in order to regenerate and replace damaged or diseased cells, tissues, and organs. Furthermore, this field may offer unprecedented potential for the treatment of previously intractable diseases, such as cancer and genetic disorders.

Sheng Lin-Gibson, who serves as chief of the Biosystems and Biomaterials Division at NIST, stated that the agency was thrilled to announce these new partnerships for the development of an innovative standards education program. This program is expected to pave the way for flexible and immersive learning experiences that support advanced biomanufacturing. Additionally, these educational programs are intended to facilitate the adoption of standards and best practices, which can often increase the quality and consistency of advanced therapies and ultimately may contribute to a reduction in costs.

The organizations that will receive these awards are Brammer Bio, which is a part of Thermo Fisher Scientific's Patheon Pharma Services, and the Standards Coordinating Body for Gene, Cell and Regenerative Medicines and Cell-Based Drug Discovery, which is a nonprofit organization based in Gaithersburg, Maryland. These organizations will produce a wide range of training opportunities, and these opportunities tend to include traditional classroom and hands-on teaching, self-paced e-learning, and the use of digital tools, multimedia resources, and immersive augmented reality. Ultimately, this initiative appears to represent a coordinated effort to strengthen standards implementation across the regenerative medicine workforce.

title: https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2023/03/cracking-metal-3d-printing-conundrum-researchers-propel-technology-toward
input:
Researchers may have not yet fully mastered the additive manufacturing process, commonly referred to as 3D printing, of metals. Gaps in the understanding of the internal dynamics of metal during this process have resulted in inconsistent outcomes. However, a recent breakthrough has the potential to provide an unprecedented level of control over metal 3D printing.

Utilizing two distinct particle accelerator facilities, scientists from the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Sweden, and various other institutions have conducted an in-depth examination of the internal structure of steel during the melting and solidifying phases of 3D printing. The results of their research, published in the journal Acta Materialia, introduce a computational tool that can significantly enhance the predictive and controlling capabilities of 3D-printing professionals regarding the characteristics of printed components. This advancement may improve the consistency and overall feasibility of this technology for large-scale manufacturing applications.

A prevalent technique for fabricating metal components involves the sequential welding of powdered metal using lasers, layer by layer, to achieve a specified shape. In the initial phases of printing with a metal alloy, the material experiences rapid heating and cooling, causing its atoms, which can consist of various elements, to form ordered, crystalline structures. These crystals play a critical role in determining essential properties, such as toughness and corrosion resistance, of the finished part. Different crystal structures can develop, each exhibiting unique advantages and disadvantages.

It is worth noting that, according to NIST physicist Fan Zhang, who co-authored the study, controlling the microstructure during the initial stages of the printing process may lead to the formation of desired crystals and ultimately dictate the performance of additively manufactured components.

Although the printing process tends to minimize material waste and enables the production of more complex shapes compared to traditional manufacturing methods, researchers continue to encounter challenges in guiding metal toward specific types of crystal structures. In summary, the advancements presented in this research may pave the way for improved consistency and functionality in metal 3D printing.

Using two different particle accelerator facilities, researchers at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Sweden and other institutions have peered into the internal structure of steel as it was melted and then solidified during 3D printing. The findings, published in Acta Materialia, unlock a computational tool for 3D-printing professionals, offering them a greater ability to predict and control the characteristics of printed parts, potentially improving the technology’s consistency and feasibility for large-scale manufacturing.

A common approach for printing metal pieces involves essentially welding pools of powdered metal with lasers, layer by layer, into a desired shape. During the first steps of printing with a metal alloy, wherein the material rapidly heats up and cools off, its atoms — which can be a smattering of different elements — pack into ordered, crystalline formations. The crystals determine the properties, such as toughness and corrosion resistance, of the printed part. Different crystal structures can emerge, each with their own pros and cons.

“Basically, if we can control the microstructure during the initial steps of the printing process, then we can obtain the desired crystals and, ultimately, determine the performance of additively manufactured parts,” said NIST physicist Fan Zhang, a study co-author.

While the printing process wastes less material and can be used to produce more complicated shapes than traditional manufacturing methods, researchers have struggled to grasp how to steer metal toward particular kinds of crystals over others.

title: https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2024/09/nist-funds-climate-measurements-center-excellence-university-vermont
input:
Additionally, it is worth noting that the U.S. Department of Commerce's National Institute of Standards and Technology has reached a decision to enter into a cooperative agreement with the University of Vermont. Furthermore, this agreement includes the provision of an award of $2.7 million, which was appropriated by Congress for the purpose of establishing a Climate Measurements Center of Excellence, following a competitive process that was announced earlier in the year. 

Notably, the primary objective of this initiative is to advance trust in measurements and technology in service to the nation, as stated by Chuck Romine, the associate director for laboratory programs at NIST, who emphasized that effective measurements are key to understanding the dynamics of complex climate systems. Ultimately, the establishment of this center of excellence may amplify the impact of climate research and enable the development of equitable climate adaptation plans. 

In essence, climate impacts tend to vary significantly from one region of the U.S. to another, and communities often require more granular information than is currently available in order to develop effective adaptation plans. Moreover, the Climate Measurements Center of Excellence is expected to support communities by providing standards frameworks, regional data, and the necessary tools for decision-making, which can often facilitate the development of informed climate strategies. 

It is worth noting that climate impacts at the community level appear to be diverse, complex, and interrelated, and may include diminished agricultural productivity, poor air quality, increased food costs, supply chain and commercial logistics disruptions, and public health issues, among other possible effects. Additionally, preparing for and mitigating these impacts can often be a challenging task for any one community alone, which tends to underscore the need for collaborative efforts. 

Ultimately, the center will bring local climate researchers together to share resources and ideas, and will serve as a hub for stakeholders, including government climate offices, universities, nonprofits, industry, and NIST, thereby facilitating the exchange of information and expertise. In summary, the establishment of the Climate Measurements Center of Excellence is a significant development that may contribute to the advancement of climate research and the development of effective climate adaptation plans, and it is likely to have a positive impact on communities across the U.S.

title: https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2022/09/nist-awards-funding-small-businesses-advance-technologies-covid-response
input:
Advent Diamond Inc., located in Scottsdale, Arizona, has developed a $100,000 phosphorous-doped quantum diamond material designed for electrical-readout quantum measurements. This new quantum material incorporates a layer of phosphorus-doped diamond, making it applicable for quantum technologies such as sensors based on nitrogen-vacancy centers. Near-term applications of this technology may include measuring magnetic fields relevant for research, space-based initiatives, and defense.

Criticality Sciences Inc., based in Alexandria, Virginia, has also received a $100,000 investment for a software tool focused on network resilience against cascading failures. This tool is intended to deliver scalable and affordable resilience metrics alongside mitigation and recovery guidance, which can assist utilities and communities in enhancing their resilience to infrastructure failures that may occur in cascading scenarios.

InfraTrac Inc., situated in Silver Spring, Maryland, has developed a $100,000 analytical quality management system aimed at 3D-printed small molecule drugs. This nondestructive testing technique utilizes near-infrared spectroscopy to evaluate the quality of in-pharmacy 3D drug printing processes, thereby supporting the formulation of customized pharmaceuticals.

Julia Jean LLC, located in Irvine, California, aims to streamline lithography processes with a $100,000 project focused on scalable electron emission from microfabricated porous silicon carbide. This initiative seeks to advance a technology patented by the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) for an electron field emitter that operates without the need for traditional heating elements. Potential applications of this technology may include advancements in lithography, electron microscopy, X-ray technology, radar, and microwave communications.

NuPhy Inc., based in Pullman, Washington, received $100,000 for its TreeTracker project, which offers an intelligent plant production optimization software platform that is cloud-capable. This platform is designed to provide insights that can assist users in optimizing plant growth, maximizing production output, and minimizing costs associated with the cultivation of new plants.

Refined Imaging LLC, located in Baton Rouge, Louisiana, has secured $100,000 for a technique that aims to establish cyber-physical trust anchors with definable costs and security features. This technique is intended to help safeguard against counterfeit manufactured components by linking a physical part to a secure database protected using blockchain technology. Collectively, these projects demonstrate a range of innovative approaches across various sectors, highlighting advancements in technology and resilience.

To continue making smartphones, laptops, and other devices more powerful and energy efficient, industry is intensely focused on identifying promising next-generation designs and materials for the principal building blocks of modern electronics: the tiny electrical on-off switches known as field-effect transistors (FETs). When deciding how to direct billions of funding dollars for next-generation transistors, investors will base many of their decisions on published research results.

But a dismaying amount of research on FETs currently suffers from inconsistent reporting and benchmarking of results, increasing risks of misleading conclusions and inaccurate claims that set false expectations for the field. This problem and possible solutions are outlined in an article published today by an international group of leading experts on semiconductor devices

“Industry is trying to determine the right materials and designs to use,” said Curt Richter, a physicist at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) and a co-author of the new article. “They want to know exactly what to make and how to make it. But the industry is getting terribly frustrated, they tell us, because they see a promising piece of information in one publication and another promising piece in another publication, but they’re incompatible. They have no way to compare them. Given the enormous cost of adopting design innovations, the industry can’t afford to make a mistake. What they want is uniform benchmarking.”

Richter, former NIST associate Zhihui Cheng(now at Intel), and Aaron Franklin of Duke University are leading an effort to create and promote guidelines for uniform test methods and reporting standards. They and more than a dozen colleagues from industry, academia, and government labs describe their recommendations in an article published today in Nature Electronics.

title: https://www.nist.gov/news-events/news/2024/08/nist-releases-first-3-finalized-post-quantum-encryption-standards
input:
The National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), which operates under the U.S. Department of Commerce, has recently concluded the development of its primary set of encryption algorithms, which are intended to resist potential cyberattacks originating from quantum computers. 

Researchers globally are engaged in a competitive effort to create quantum computers that may function in fundamentally different manners compared to traditional computers. Such advancements could potentially compromise the effectiveness of current encryption methods that are crucial for ensuring security and privacy across various online activities. The encryption algorithms that NIST has announced today are detailed within the initial set of completed standards derived from NIST’s post-quantum cryptography (PQC) standardization project, and they are available for immediate application.

Furthermore, these three new standards are designed with a forward-looking perspective. The technology associated with quantum computing is advancing swiftly, and some experts estimate that a device capable of undermining existing encryption techniques could emerge within the next decade. This development poses significant risks to the security and privacy of individuals, organizations, and nations alike.

It is worth noting that the progression of quantum computing holds substantial implications for reaffirming America’s position as a leading technological entity while also influencing the future of economic security. Deputy Secretary of Commerce Don Graves emphasized this point by stating, “The advancement of quantum computing plays an essential role in reaffirming America’s status as a global technological powerhouse and driving the future of our economic security.” He further remarked that the various bureaus within the Department of Commerce are committed to ensuring U.S. competitiveness in the quantum domain, particularly through the efforts of NIST, which is taking a proactive stance in this comprehensive governmental initiative. 

NIST is contributing critical expertise toward the development of innovative approaches to quantum-related challenges, including security strategies such as post-quantum cryptography that organizations can begin to adopt for safeguarding their future in a post-quantum landscape. As this extensive endeavor progresses over the next decade, there is optimism about advancing the legacy of leadership that the Department of Commerce has established in this essential area.

In essence, the reporting of research results must be done in a manner that takes into account the specific context of the transistor's dimensions and materials. And if your research gets a different answer, you have to work ten times harder to overcome the effect of the first publication.”
